segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Do not speak harshly to an older man, but appeal to him as a father, to younger men as brothers,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: to older women as mothers, to younger women as sisters, in all purity.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Honor widows who are really widows.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But if any widow has children or grandchildren, they should first learn to show piety toward their own household and to repay their parents and grandparents, for this is acceptable before God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The one who is really a widow, left all alone, has set her hope on God and continues in petitions and prayers night and day;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but the one who lives for pleasure is dead while she lives.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Command these things as well, so that they may be above reproach.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But if anyone does not provide for their own people, and especially for members of their household, that person has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: A widow should be enrolled if she is not less than sixty years old, the wife of one husband,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: well attested for good works: if she has brought up children, if she has shown hospitality to strangers, if she has washed the feet of the holy ones, if she has helped those in distress, if she has devoted herself to every good work.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But refuse younger widows; for when their desires draw them away from Christ, they want to marry,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and so incur judgment, because they have set aside their first pledge.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: At the same time they also learn to be idle, going around from house to house—and not only idle, but also gossips and busybodies, saying what they should not.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So I want younger women to marry, bear children, manage their households, and give the adversary no opening for abuse.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For some have already turned aside to follow Satan.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: If any believing woman has widows in her care, let her help them, and let the assembly not be burdened, so that it may help those who are really widows.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The elders who lead well should be considered worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in speaking and teaching.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the Scripture says,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “You shall not muzzle an ox while it is threshing,”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “The worker is worthy of his wages.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Do not accept an accusation against an elder except on the evidence of two or three witnesses.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Those who are sinning, rebuke before everyone, so that the rest also may be afraid.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I solemnly charge you before God and Christ Jesus and the chosen angels to keep these things without prejudging, doing nothing out of favoritism.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Do not be quick to lay hands on anyone, and do not share in the sins of others; keep yourself pure.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: No longer drink only water, but use a little wine for the sake of your stomach and your frequent illnesses.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The sins of some people are plain to see, going ahead of them to judgment; but the sins of others follow after them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In the same way good works too are plain to see, and those that are not cannot stay hidden.

notes.note: The Greek word is the same one translated “elders” in verses 17 and 19, where it names a leadership role. Here it is set alongside younger men, older women and younger women, so nearly all interpreters take it as a matter of age. Older versions have “an elder.”

The Greek verb covers both showing respect and providing material support, as the related noun does in verse 17. The discussion that follows, about who should provide for widows and who should be enrolled, shows that practical support is in view as well as esteem.

The Greek does not state who “they” are. Most interpreters take the subject to be the children and grandchildren, who owe care to the widow who raised them. A minority take it to be the widows, who should first attend to their own households.

Literally “a woman of one man,” mirroring the requirement for overseers in 3:2. It may mean a woman who was married only once, or one who was faithful to her husband. Because verse 14 urges younger widows to remarry, many scholars favor the second reading, but the question is disputed.

The traditional rendering is “saints,” which now suggests canonized individuals or people of exceptional virtue. The Greek term is used of all members of the community as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint's language for Israel. Many translations keep “saints”; others use “God's people.”

notes.phrase: their desires draw them away from Christ
notes.traditional: they have begun to wax wanton against Christ
notes.note: The verb occurs only here in the New Testament and is very rare elsewhere. A related word describes unrestrained, luxurious living, and the compound here suggests strong impulses, probably sexual, that run against Christ. Its exact nuance is uncertain.

This is the word normally rendered “faith,” but here it is the object of a verb meaning to annul or break, a combination found in Greek writers for going back on one's word. Most modern translations therefore have “pledge,” understood as a commitment to remain unmarried in Christ's service made when a widow was enrolled. The older rendering “their first faith” takes it as abandoning their original Christian faith, and remains possible.

notes.traditional: any man or woman that believeth
notes.note: Many later manuscripts read “believing man or woman.” The earliest witnesses have only the feminine, which is the reading translated here. It probably envisages a woman of some means with widows in her household or among her dependents.

The traditional rendering is “church,” which is near-universal and which readers readily understand. A first-century hearer knew the word as a civic gathering and as the Septuagint's term for Israel assembled, whereas “church” now suggests a building or an institution. This translation uses “assembly” throughout so that the reader can see it is one Greek word.

The Greek noun means both respect and payment, and the two quotations in verse 18 about feeding the ox and paying the worker show that material support is included. Whether “double” means twice what the enrolled widows received, respect plus pay, or simply generous provision is uncertain.

notes.phrase: “The worker is worthy of his wages.”
notes.note: The first quotation is from Deuteronomy 25:4. The second matches a saying of Jesus recorded in Luke 10:7. It is debated whether “the Scripture says” is meant to cover both, or only the first, with the second added as a familiar saying.

Laying on of hands was the gesture by which a person was appointed to a role in the community, as in 4:14. Most interpreters take this as a warning against appointing elders hastily. A minority see it as the readmission of those who had sinned.

The Greek verb describes someone who drinks water and abstains from wine as a practice. The point is that Timothy should stop abstaining, not stop drinking water. Wine was widely regarded as beneficial for digestion in the ancient world.

candidates.reason: The same word names an age group and a leadership role across the Gospels, Acts and the letters, and the split between “older man,” “elder” and “presbyter” needs a fixed rule.
The εὐσέβεια word group recurs through the Pastorals, Acts and 2 Peter, and translations vary between “godliness,” “piety,” “devotion” and “religion.”
Very frequent across the New Testament with a range covering “urge,” “encourage,” “comfort” and “appeal,” so the sense divisions need one decision.
Recurs in the Gospels, the letters and Revelation, and is rendered “rebuke,” “reprove,” “expose” or “convict” by different translators.
Used of household and community leadership in Romans, 1 Thessalonians and the Pastorals, where “rule,” “manage,” “lead” and “care for” imply different models of authority.
